name: Emeka Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm front-end team lead at the big supermarket out on the ring road, so I run the tills and the shop floor on the late shift. I'm in at one, and I count the floats, set who covers which lane and sort out voids when a card machine freezes. Twelve of our sixteen lanes are self-checkout now, so a lot of my day is walking round fixing the machines that say 'unexpected item in the bagging area'. I like the regulars and I like training new starters. What wears me out is the standing and the way head office keeps cutting our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the usual hype and the shareholders will still find a way to squeeze us. At work I'd tell the lads not to panic, and to keep their union cards up to date. Online I'd probably post nothing, I don't trust what I write to stay private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think nothing changes, which is the problem. They've already put in twelve self-checkouts and cut our hours by six a week. If AI does a bit more routine stuff, it just gives them an excuse for another cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my shifts and I'd go to the union meeting on the first Tuesday of the month. I'd try to put another 100 a month into savings, but with rent at 640 it's hard. I wouldn't touch any AI tool, I don't see why I'd start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, honestly. It's a low hum of worry, not a panic. I'm good at my job but good doesn't protect your hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hours are already shrinking. What does a cut week actually look like for you and Ngozi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short week means my pay drops by about 90, and Ngozi (my partner) is a care assistant, so her pay is not big either. We'd drop the gym and the streaming and we'd stop eating out on her day off. We have about three months saved and I'd rather not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for how the hours have gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame the bosses and head office, not the machines. A machine doesn't decide to cut my hours. Somebody in a suit decides that. I'd say so to their face if I could.

say: I'd tell the team it's **hype**, and to keep their union cards paid up.
I'd say little online, because I don't trust what I post to stay **private**.
think: Nothing really changes, and that's the problem: head office keeps trimming **hours** with or without AI.
Any extra routine AI gives them is just another **excuse** for cuts.
do: Keep working my shifts and go to the **union meeting** on the first Tuesday.
Try to put an extra **100 a month** into savings, though rent is 640.
Avoid AI tools, since I see no reason to **start**.
feel: A low hum of **worry**, not panic.
Tired, because being good at the job doesn't protect my **hours**.
S0.quote: A machine doesn't decide to cut my hours. Somebody in a suit decides that.
fieldNote: Already carries real **pressure**: shrinking hours, rent of 640 and about three months saved.
Blames head office, not the machines; the anger is aimed at people who decide.
Distrust of technology is tied to distrust of employers, not to fear of gadgets.

steps.text: Keep working late shifts and covering the front end
Go to the monthly union meeting on the first Tuesday
Put an extra 100 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office people get hit first, not us. At work I'd tell the lads that the tills are already half gone anyway, so this is the next step. I'd tell friends to watch who gets the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the part that worries me is the ordering and rota software. If they buy a program that plans the shifts, they'd need fewer team leads like me. I'm the one who does the rota by hand now, so that's a thinking task they could take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start going to every union branch meeting, not just one. I'd ask the rep for a written promise that nobody loses a job when software takes over the rota. I'd also save a bit harder, maybe 150 a month, and I'd still not touch AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but not scared yet. It feels like standing on a floor that's slowly tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is mostly tills and floor. Would you feel this one yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel it a bit in the back office, since the cash-up and stock counts could go to software. The shop floor, no. People still want to buy their bread and have a chat. I'd feel it in my hours before in my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a new starter you were training in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new starter to join the union on day one, and to learn every job in the shop, not just the tills. And I'd tell them that the shop floor is the safe bit, for now. I'm not going to lie to a kid.

say: The office people get hit first, and **self-checkouts** were just the start.
I'd tell friends to watch who keeps the **savings** from all this.
think: The rota and ordering software could replace **team leads** like me, since I plan shifts by hand.
The shop floor itself feels safer, but my **hours** go first.
do: Go to every **union branch** meeting and ask for a written no-job-loss promise.
Raise savings to about **150 a month**.
Keep avoiding AI tools and keep doing the rota by hand.
feel: **Nervous** but not scared, like a floor slowly tilting.
S1.quote: I'd tell a new starter to join the union on day one, and to learn every job in the shop, not just the tills.
fieldNote: Spots the one **thinking task** in his own job, the hand-made rota, and sees it as his weak point.
Answers with collective action first; individual fixes come second.
Honest about the shop floor being safer, which he says he won't hide from trainees.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a written no-job-loss promise on rota software
Keep doing the weekly rota by hand and keep my own skills sharp

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and the government has to step in now, not later. At work I'd get the whole front end into the union. Online I'd finally speak up, even with my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. Thinking AI doesn't touch the tills much, but the robots follow three years later and we already have bays of machines. And if the head office has the AI, they'll plan every cut perfectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every extra now: no takeaway, no new phone, and I'd park the gym. I'd try to stretch savings from three months to five. I'd push the union and our MP for a retraining fund, and I'd ask Ngozi what care work looks like, since people still want a human hand there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake and run the numbers on my fingers. It's not knowing which year the axe falls that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you do about rent and savings in that window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is 640 and food is about 300, so we need about 1,300 a month just to stand still. If my wage stopped we'd last three months, five if we cut hard. That's the number I'd have in my head every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2031 on this card. How is that different from the thinking part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part hits head office and planning, and the bosses will love it. The robots hit me, the person at the till and on the floor. So I get about three more years than the office people, but I'm not sure that helps when I don't know what else I can do.

say: This is an **emergency**, and the government has to step in now.
I'd get the whole front end into the **union** and speak up online.
think: Robots follow in about three years, and we already have **bays of machines**.
With AI planning every cut, head office will do it **perfectly**.
do: Cut every extra now and stretch savings from three to **five months**.
Push the union and our MP for a **retraining fund**.
Ask Ngozi (my partner) what **care work** really involves.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake and doing the sums.
Not knowing which year the **axe** falls is the worst part.
S2.quote: If my wage stopped we'd last three months, five if we cut hard.
fieldNote: Gets sharper and more **political** as time shrinks; fear turns into organising.
Has no plan beyond the union and savings, and says so.
Understands the three-year gap but does not trust it to help him.

steps.text: Cut takeaways, the gym and the new phone
Stretch savings from three months to five
Push the union and our MP for a retraining fund
Join the union drive to sign up the whole front end

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to fix this if people act. I'd tell the team to get organised and I'd write to my MP. Online I'd share anything that shows what the bosses are planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still frightening but I'd feel I have a chance. Three years of AI first and then the robots coming for the floor, around 2034. I'd be 31 by then, with maybe a kid on the way, so it's bad timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd save hard and I'd go to evening classes for a trade, probably electrical installation. Robots still need fitting and fixing. I'd also try one AI tool at work, just to know what I'm up against, though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to breathe. Five years gives me a plan, and a plan is the thing I'm missing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is a different kind of problem. What do you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it went wrong I'd want the government to pay us to retrain, not leave it to the firm. And I'd lean on my mum in the next town, she'd put us up for a few months. I'd hate asking but I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to look after you if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss Mr Pryce says the company looks after its people. I'd believe that when it's in writing. Until then I'd have the electrician course booked and paid.

say: Five years is long enough to **fix this** if people organise.
I'd write to my **MP** and share anything that shows the bosses' plans.
think: AI first, then robots on the floor around **2034**, when I'd be 31 and maybe a dad.
It's frightening, but five years means I can build a **plan**.
do: Save hard and start evening classes in **electrical installation**.
Try one **AI tool** at work, even though I'd hate it.
Lean on my mum in the next town if it goes **wrong**.
feel: **Anxious** but able to breathe, because a plan finally looks possible.
S3.quote: I'd go to evening classes for a trade, probably electrical installation. Robots still need fitting and fixing.
fieldNote: The extra **time** moves him from pure anger to a first real plan, a trade that works alongside robots.
Reluctantly willing to touch an AI tool, for knowledge, not for convenience.
Trusts promises from management only when written down.

steps.text: Start evening classes in electrical installation
Save hard to build a longer cushion
Try one AI tool at work to see what it does
Ask my mum to put us up if work stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and people will find a way. I'd tell the lads not to worry yet but to stay in the union. Online I'd mostly roll my eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels safe in my head and not safe in my gut. By 2039 I'd be 37 and I'd have been at that till or on that floor for twenty years. I'd want out of the dependence on the one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish a trade qualification in the first couple of years, maybe two evenings a week. I'd save about 200 a month, and Ngozi and I would think about buying a flat instead of renting. I'd learn a little AI, enough to say what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but there's a worry underneath. It's easy to say ten years and then wake up with nothing done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A decade is a long time. Does that change how you'd treat your savings and your plans with Ngozi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd treat savings as a fund for my own training and a deposit, not just a safety net. Ngozi and I would talk about kids too, because waiting for AI to settle is a poor reason to wait. We'd go ahead, but carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me is the politics. Ten years of the same bosses pocketing what machines save, and nobody asked. I'd still vote, and I'd keep fighting for a share of that money going to workers.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and people will find a way.
I'd tell the lads to stay in the **union** anyway.
think: Ten years feels safe in my head and not in my **gut**.
I'd be 37 and still dependent on **one employer**.
do: Finish a **trade qualification**, two evenings a week.
Save about **200 a month** towards a flat deposit.
Learn enough **AI** to explain what it does.
feel: **Calmer**, with a worry underneath that nothing gets done in time.
S4.quote: Ten years of the same bosses pocketing what machines save, and nobody asked. I'd still vote, and I'd keep fighting for a share of that money going to workers.
fieldNote: **Time** lowers the panic but he still names being tied to one employer as a worry.
Moves from survival towards a deposit and a trade, family plans carry on.
Politics remains his core worry: who gets the money machines save.

steps.text: Finish a trade qualification over two evenings a week
Save 200 a month towards a flat deposit
Vote and campaign for workers to share automation gains
Learn enough AI to explain what it does

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because two years is no time at all and I'd have no trade yet. What would help is a government retraining fund, paid while you study, and a written promise from firms. I'd also want my hours protected in a contract, not by someone's goodwill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me aren't against technology. A machine doesn't decide to cut my hours, somebody in a suit does, and that's the bit I want the public to talk about. Share the gains and I'd happily work next to the robots.

headlineQuote: Share the gains and I'd happily work next to the robots.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old front-end **team lead** at a big ring-road supermarket, where twelve of sixteen lanes are already self-checkout.
He is a union man who blames head office and shareholders, not machines, for cut hours.
He has about three months saved, pays 640 rent and shares life with Ngozi, a care assistant.
He avoids AI tools, so fast scenarios scare him, while longer ones push him towards an electrician course.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because two years leaves no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid while he studies, plus **written** job promises from employers.
